kurals.tamil:
இன்மையின் இன்னாதது யாதெனின் இன்மையின்
இன்மையே இன்னா தது.
kurals.transliteration:
Inmaiyin innaadhadhu yaadhenin inmaiyin
inmaiyae innaa thadhu.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what is more painful than poverty, the only answer is poverty itself; it has no equal among sorrows.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone asking, “What hurts more than a really bad toothache?” and the answer is, “Only a really bad toothache.” Valluvar says being so poor that you have nothing is like that: there is nothing else to compare it with, because it is the worst hurt of its kind.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a deliberately circular definition built on repetition of inmai (இன்மை, ‘not-having, want’): inmaiyin innaadhadhu (‘what is more grievous than want’) is answered by inmaiyae (‘want itself’). Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar both gloss inmaiyin as a comparative (‘like poverty’), so the sense is that poverty is its own only standard of comparison; Kalaignar makes the same point by saying no other sorrow can serve as an upamai (simile) for it. The figure is a classic Tamil ananvaya-like device in which the subject is compared to itself to mark it as incomparable, and Pope’s ‘Nothing pains more than poverty, save poverty alone’ preserves the tautology. Nalkuravu (நல்குரவு) in the chapter title is the standard classical word for destitution; placed in the Kudiyiyal right after Uzhavu (ch. 104, agriculture, the remedy for want) and before Iravu (ch. 106, begging), the chapter traces the social consequences of losing one’s means. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net apart from spacing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The man that is fallen, O king, grieveth, as also he that is poor. I do not see the difference between a fallen man and a poor man.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna, urging Yudhishthira not to renounce his kingdom, argues that poverty is a misery equal to moral or social ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Arjuna treats poverty as a sorrow that has no lesser comparison than utter downfall.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong thematic fit, though it is Arjuna’s partisan argument rather than a settled teaching of the epic.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The rich man’s wealth is his strong city: the destruction of the poor is their poverty.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes that the poor man’s ruin is nothing other than his poverty itself, while wealth is a fortress.
christianity.tie_back: The proverb’s tautology, the poor are destroyed by their poverty, mirrors the Kural’s ‘poverty is worse than anything but poverty’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; close in both idea and self-referential form.

islam.quote_or_event: “O Allah, I seek refuge in Thee from poverty”, lack and abasement, and I seek refuge in Thee lest I cause or suffer wrong.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet regularly sought God’s protection from poverty, naming it alongside want and humiliation as evils to be shielded from.
islam.tie_back: Seeking refuge from poverty itself shows it was regarded, as in the Kural, as among the gravest afflictions.
islam.source: Sunan Abi Dawud 1544 (graded sahih by al-Albani)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com including its odd quotation mark; it treats poverty as a dire evil but does not rank it above all others.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is nothing in the world as harsh as poverty, as it is harsher than all the suffering in the world. Our Rabbis said: All forms of suffering on one side, and poverty on the other.”
judaism.explanation: The Midrash weighs every other suffering on one side of the scale and poverty alone on the other, and finds poverty heavier.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost exactly Valluvar’s claim that nothing is as painful as poverty.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match of the central claim.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hunger is the worst disease, conditioned things the worst suffering.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada names hunger, the most immediate face of want, as the worst of illnesses, before turning to the deeper suffering of conditioned existence.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts single out want of food and means as a misery beyond comparison.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it speaks of hunger rather than poverty in general and points beyond it to the suffering of all conditioned things.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though emaciated like the joint of a crow’s (leg) and covered with a network of veins, he should know the permitted measure of food and drink, and wander about with a cheerful mind.”
jainism.explanation: Among the troubles (parishaha) a monk must bear, Mahavira lists hunger, and asks the monk to accept even extreme emaciation cheerfully.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural calls want the worst pain, Jain discipline treats chosen want as a trial to be borne with a calm mind, an instructive contrast.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrast rather than a parallel, since it concerns voluntary ascetic hunger, not involuntary destitution.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...he left Aeolian Cyme and fled, not from riches and substance, but from wretched poverty which Zeus lays upon men...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod recalls that his father abandoned his homeland and crossed the sea simply to escape poverty, which he presents as a burden laid on men by Zeus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The flight shows poverty as an affliction so heavy that a man will give up his home to escape it, echoing the Kural’s estimate of its pain.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 633-640 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shows how dreaded poverty was, but does not explicitly rank it above all other sorrows.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But if you are averse to sickness, or death, or poverty, you will be wretched.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus warns that fearing things outside our control, poverty among them, is what makes people miserable.
philosophy.tie_back: The Stoic answers the Kural from the other side: poverty is painful above all to the one who judges it an evil.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a deliberate counterpoint, not an endorsement of the Kural’s claim.

kurals.tamil:
இன்மை எனவொரு பாவி மறுமையும்
இம்மையும் இன்றி வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inmai enavoru paavi maRumaiyum
immaiyum indri varum.
kurals.meaning: The wicked one called poverty, once it comes, robs a person of both the joys of this life and the good of the next.
kurals.elementary: Think of a villain in a story who sneaks in and takes away both your lunch today and your treat for tomorrow. Valluvar calls poverty a villain like that: it takes away the good things you could enjoy now, and also the good you could do for others, which helps you later.
kurals.university: Valluvar personifies inmai as oru paavi (ஒரு பாவி), ‘a sinner, a wicked one’, a vivid figure for an abstract condition. The second line says it comes so that maRumai (மறுமை, the next world) and immai (இம்மை, this world) are both lost. Solomon Pappaiah spells out the logic the commentators share: the poor cannot give to others, so they lose the merit that secures the next world, and they have nothing to enjoy themselves, so they lose this world too; Puliyur Kesikan likewise speaks of losing worldly pleasure here and the bliss of heaven hereafter. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads the pair temporally (present and future), and Kalaignar secularises it as loss of peace now and later. The Kural thus ties wealth to aram (virtue) through the duty of giving, a link developed in the Arathuppaal chapters on Eekai (giving) and Oppuravu (helpfulness). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that is without wealth hath neither this world, nor the next, O best of men!”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna argues that without wealth a person can neither enjoy life nor perform the religious acts that secure the hereafter.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost word for word the Kural’s claim that poverty takes away both this world and the next.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near one-to-one match, though voiced by Arjuna in a debate rather than as final doctrine.

christianity.quote_or_event: “So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs pictures poverty arriving like a traveller or an armed robber who overpowers the idle.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s ‘wicked one’, poverty is personified as an intruder that comes and takes away.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; shares the personification but not the loss of both worlds.

islam.quote_or_event: “And He found you poor and made [you] self-sufficient.”
islam.explanation: God reminds the Prophet that he too was once poor, and that his poverty did not cut him off from divine favour.
islam.tie_back: The verse quietly counters the Kural: in Islam poverty need not cost a person the next world.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on alquran.cloud; a contrasting next-best match rather than a parallel.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Three classes of people do not see the face of Gehenna... Those suffering the depths of extreme poverty, those afflicted with intestinal disease, and those oppressed by creditors.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud teaches that the suffering of extreme poverty atones for sin, so the very poor are spared Gehenna.
judaism.tie_back: Where the Kural says poverty loses the next world, the rabbis hold that it can secure it, a pointed contrast on the same question.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Eruvin 41b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (ellipsis marks omitted Steinsaltz gloss); it addresses the same this-world/next-world question but reaches the opposite conclusion.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “But one with confidence, living at home, making gifts of his belongings, righteously-gained, wins both goals: advantage in the here-&-now, & happiness in the world beyond.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the householder who gives from rightly earned wealth as winning benefit both now and hereafter.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the mirror image of the Kural: wealth used for giving wins both worlds, so its absence forfeits both.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the ‘two worlds through giving’ logic matches Pappaiah’s reading of the Kural closely.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He will sink through anger; he will go down through pride; delusion will block up his path; through greed he will incur dangers in both worlds.”
jainism.explanation: Nami tells Indra that it is greed, not lack of wealth, that endangers a person in this world and the next.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain sage relocates the Kural’s threat to both worlds from poverty to the craving for possessions.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; same ‘both worlds’ frame, but it blames greed rather than poverty.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes’ comedy Wealth (Plutus), Poverty (Penia) appears in person as a fearsome goddess, and Chremylus resolves to drive her out of Greece as the source of men’s miseries, while she argues that she is what keeps men industrious.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek imagination, like Valluvar’s, turned poverty into a personified being who stalks human households.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penia as a menacing figure parallels the Kural’s ‘poverty, a wicked one’ who comes and takes everything.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from general knowledge of the play, not verified against a live text in this session; matches the personification only, not the loss of both worlds.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For it is better to die with hunger, exempt from grief and fear, than to live in affluence with perturbation.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus insists that peace of mind matters more than material security, even at the cost of hunger.
philosophy.tie_back: The Stoic denies the Kural’s premise that losing wealth means losing life’s good.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a counterpoint rather than a parallel.

kurals.tamil:
தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும் தொகையாக
நல்குரவு என்னும் நசை.
kurals.transliteration:
Tholvaravum thoalum kedukkum thogaiyaaga
nalkuravu ennum nasai.
kurals.meaning: The hungry craving called poverty destroys, all at once, a family’s ancient standing and its good name.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a family that has been known for generations as kind and honest. If someone in it becomes so desperate that wanting things takes over, they might do things that spoil the family’s good name all at once, like one spill ruining a whole painting.
kurals.university: The key word is nasai (நசை, ‘desire, craving’): Valluvar does not just say nalkuravu but ‘nalkuravu ennum nasai’, the craving that is called poverty, suggesting that destitution shows itself as a gnawing want. Tholvaravu (தொல்வரவு) is ‘what has come down from of old’, the dignity or heritage of one’s line, and thoal (தோல்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan as pugazh (fame, honour); the English explanation carried on ytamizh.com renders it ‘the dignity of one’s speech’, reflecting an older reading that associates thoal with elevated, well-formed words. Thogaiyaaga (‘all together, at a stroke’) stresses the suddenness of the ruin. Kalaignar shifts the causation slightly, saying that poverty breeds greed which then ruins lineage and fame. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It is lust only, Arjuna, which is born of contact with the material mode of passion and later transformed into wrath, and which is the all-devouring sinful enemy of this world.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna identifies kama, craving, as the all-consuming enemy that degrades a person.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s nasai, the craving that comes with poverty, is the same all-devouring desire the Gita warns can destroy what a person has built.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.37 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it concerns desire in general, not poverty or family honour.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that the craving to become rich drags people into ruinous desires.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see a desperate hunger for wealth as what wrecks a person’s standing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it addresses craving for riches rather than the craving born of poverty, and says nothing of lineage.

islam.quote_or_event: “But when He tries him and restricts his provision, he says, ‘My Lord has humiliated me.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes how a person whose provision is narrowed feels himself disgraced, though the verse then corrects this view.
islam.tie_back: The felt loss of honour that comes with straitened means is exactly what the Kural describes.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on alquran.cloud; it matches the sense of lost dignity, but the Qur’an rejects the idea that poverty is real humiliation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is rich? He who rejoices in his lot.”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines wealth as contentment, so the restless craving for more is itself a kind of poverty.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural calls poverty a nasai, a craving; the Mishnah answers that the cure lies in rejoicing in one’s portion.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (tr. Dr. Joshua Kulp, Mishnah Yomit)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; it addresses craving, not the loss of family honour.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, free from avarice amidst the avaricious. Amidst the avaricious men we dwell free from avarice.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises those who live free of craving even among the grasping.
buddhism.tie_back: Against the Kural’s ruinous nasai, the Buddhist ideal is freedom from that very craving.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a contrast centred on craving, with nothing on lineage or fame.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two mâshas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila, a poor Brahmin student, realised while deciding how much gold to ask a king for that his want kept swelling, and renounced the world on the spot.
jainism.tie_back: Kapila’s story shows exactly the ‘craving called poverty’ that, unchecked, ruins a man’s standing.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 8.17, with the Kapila legend in Jacobi’s note (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong fit on poverty turning into craving, though the outcome is renunciation rather than disgrace.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Erysichthon, cursed by Demeter with insatiable Hunger, devoured his whole family fortune and at last sold his own daughter Mestra to buy food.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s retelling, a hunger that could never be filled consumed an old and wealthy house and drove its head to shame his own child.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The myth dramatises the Kural’s ‘craving called poverty’ destroying a family’s heritage and honour in one sweep.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from general knowledge of Metamorphoses 8, not verified against a live text in this session; a vivid but mythic parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Don’t allow such considerations as these distress you. ‘I will live in dishonor, and be nobody anywhere.’”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the student not to fear the loss of public standing, since dishonour from outside cannot touch one’s character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural laments the loss of name and heritage; the Stoic argues that such losses are not true evils.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a counterpoint on loss of standing, not specifically about poverty.

kurals.tamil:
இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் இன்மை இளிவந்த
சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
IRpiRandhaar kaNNaeyum inmai iLivandha
soRpiRakkum soarvu tharum.
kurals.meaning: Poverty breeds, even in people of good family, a weariness from which mean and shameful words come out.
kurals.elementary: When you are very tired and hungry, you might snap at someone even though you are usually polite. Valluvar says being very poor can make even well-brought-up people so worn down that unkind or embarrassing words slip out.
kurals.university: IRpiRandhaar (இற்பிறந்தார்) are ‘those born in a (good) house’, i.e. of noble family, and the -um of kaNNaeyum (‘even in them’) concedes that breeding is no protection. Inmai gives soarvu (சோர்வு, ‘slackness, exhaustion, lapse of vigilance’) from which iLivandha sol (இளிவந்த சொல், ‘words that bring disgrace’) is born. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it this way: poverty causes the lapse, and the lapse produces demeaning speech. Puliyur Kesikan, notably, reverses the causation, saying that the slackness which leads to base acts is itself what brings poverty even to good families, a reading that turns the couplet into a warning rather than a lament. Pope’s ‘Oblivion that gives birth to words that bring disgrace’ takes soarvu as forgetfulness of one’s station. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “King Nahusha, having done many wicked acts in a state of poverty, cried fie on that state and said that poverty is for recluses.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna cites the royal Nahusha, who was driven to wicked acts when reduced to poverty.
hinduism.tie_back: Even a king of illustrious line fell into base conduct through want, just as the Kural says of those nobly born.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong fit, with wicked acts in place of the Kural’s shameful words.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me: Lest I be full, and deny thee... or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.”
christianity.explanation: Agur prays to be spared poverty because it might push him to steal and to profane God’s name.
christianity.tie_back: The prayer names exactly the Kural’s danger: want driving a decent person to shameful deeds and words.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted words); a close match, including the element of debased speech.

islam.quote_or_event: “Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an pairs the fear of poverty with the pull toward shameful conduct, both ascribed to Satan’s whispering.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees poverty, or the dread of it, as the doorway to disgraceful behaviour.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on alquran.cloud; strong thematic fit, though it speaks of the threat of poverty rather than poverty itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Three matters cause a person to act against his own will and the will of his Maker, and they are: Gentiles, and an evil spirit, and the depths of extreme poverty.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud lists crushing poverty among forces that make a person act against both his own nature and God’s will, and therefore asks that we pray for such people.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point precisely: poverty can make even the well-born behave unlike themselves.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Eruvin 41b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (bracketing of the translator’s bold text removed); a close match on the mechanism.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Cakkavatti Sihanada Sutta the Buddha relates how a king who failed to give wealth to the destitute let poverty spread, and from poverty came theft, then weapons, killing and lying, so that a whole people sank into degraded conduct.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta traces a causal chain in which poverty is the first step toward social and moral collapse.
buddhism.tie_back: It extends the Kural’s point from one family to a whole society: want breeds base acts and base words, including lying.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known narrative; the accesstoinsight.org page available in this session is only an excerpt without this passage, so no wording is quoted.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A houseless and poor monk who wanders from village to village may become tired of ascetic life: he should bear this trouble.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira names discontent (arati), the weariness of the poor wandering monk, as a trouble to be recognised and overcome.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism acknowledges the very soarvu (weariness) the Kural describes, but asks that it be mastered rather than allowed to degrade one.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable parallel on poverty-induced weariness, without the element of shameful speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “An evil shame is the needy man’s companion, shame which both greatly harms and prospers men: shame is with poverty, but confidence with wealth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod observes that need brings with it a crippling sense of shame, while wealth brings confidence.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both poets see poverty as robbing a person of the dignity that normally governs speech and conduct.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 317-319 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong fit, though Hesiod stresses shame felt rather than shameful words spoken.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Wealth, I said, and poverty; the one is the parent of luxury and indolence, and the other of meanness and viciousness, and both of discontent.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells Adeimantus that poverty breeds meanness and vice, which is why the guardians must keep both extremes out of the city.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato’s ‘poverty, the parent of meanness’ is the Kural’s claim that want gives birth to base conduct.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a close match on poverty generating meanness.

kurals.tamil:
நல்குரவு என்னும் இடும்பையுள் பல்குரைத்
துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nalkuravu ennum idumbaiyuL palkuraith
thunbangaL sendru padum.
kurals.meaning: Within the single affliction called poverty, sorrows of every kind gather and take root.
kurals.elementary: Have you seen one leak in a roof let in rain that ruins the carpet, the books and the bed? Valluvar says poverty is like that one leak: many other troubles come pouring in through it.
kurals.university: Idumbai (இடும்பை, ‘affliction, distress’) names poverty as one trouble, and palkurai (பல்குரை, ‘of many kinds’) thunbangaL (‘sorrows’) are said to ‘go and settle’ (sendru padum) within it. Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah read this as all sorrows being contained in poverty, so that poverty is the sum of misfortunes; Mu. Varadarasanar says they ‘arise and grow’ inside it; Kalaignar reverses the image slightly, with many sorrows springing out of poverty. Either way poverty is the matrix of other ills, which prepares for the later couplets on lost respect (1046), estranged kin (1047) and sleepless dread (1048-1049). Pope’s ‘Attendant sorrows plenteous grow’ follows the ‘springing up’ reading. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The acts of a person who, possessed of little intelligence, suffers himself to be divested of wealth, are all dried up like shallow streams in the summer season.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna argues that once wealth is lost every undertaking withers, like streams in summer.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the loss of means is not one trouble but the drying-up of everything else.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a good fit on cascading loss, though framed around a man who lets his wealth slip.

christianity.quote_or_event: “All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs observes that for the afflicted every day brings trouble.
christianity.tie_back: The afflicted person’s days filled with evils echo the Kural’s many sorrows gathered in poverty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the ‘afflicted’ (Hebrew ʿani, also ‘poor’) supports the link, but the verse is general.

islam.quote_or_event: “And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an lists hunger and loss of wealth among a cluster of trials that come together.
islam.tie_back: Loss of wealth arrives alongside fear, hunger and other losses, as the Kural says many sorrows gather in poverty.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on alquran.cloud; it groups trials together but presents them as tests answered by patience.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Poverty in a person’s household is more difficult than fifty plagues.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Pinehas ben Hama, reading the friends’ words to Job, concludes that poverty at home outweighs fifty plagues.
judaism.tie_back: Fifty plagues gathered in one condition is the Kural’s ‘sorrows of every kind’ settling inside poverty.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Bava Batra 116a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match on poverty as the sum of many afflictions.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Poverty is called suffering in the world; so, too, is getting into debt. A poor person, in debt, partaking of sensuality, suffers hardship. Then they hound him and put him into bondage.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces how poverty leads to debt, interest, notices, harassment and finally bondage, one suffering after another.
buddhism.tie_back: The sutta lays out step by step how many sorrows flow into the one condition of poverty.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org (verse lines joined); the sutta then uses this chain as a metaphor for moral debt.

jainism.quote_or_event: “All men who are ignorant of the Truth are subject to pain; in the endless Samsâra they suffer in many ways.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that the root of manifold suffering is ignorance of the truth, which keeps beings bound in samsara.
jainism.tie_back: Where the Kural finds many sorrows gathered in poverty, Jainism locates their common root in spiritual ignorance.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); next-best match, sharing only the idea of manifold suffering from one root.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus says that nothing is more shameless than the hungry belly, which forces a man to remember it and drives men to endure many evils for its sake.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s hero, living as a poor wanderer, names hunger as the source of a whole train of hardships.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The beggar Odysseus shows the Kural’s point that want brings many sufferings with it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from general knowledge of the Odyssey, not verified against a live text in this session.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Of all the woes of luckless poverty none is harder to endure than this, that it exposes men to ridicule.”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal’s Umbritius catalogues the many woes of the Roman poor: high rent, torn clothes, lost legacies, contempt and danger.
philosophy.tie_back: Juvenal’s ‘woes of luckless poverty’ is a satirist’s inventory of the Kural’s many sorrows gathered in want.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on tertullian.org; Juvenal is a Roman satirist rather than a philosopher, used here as the best fit in the secular moral tradition.

kurals.tamil:
நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும் நல்கூர்ந்தார்
சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
NaRporuL nangunarndhu sollinum nalkoorndhaar
soRporuL soarvu padum.
kurals.meaning: Even when the poor speak sound truths they have fully understood, their words are disregarded and come to nothing.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two children giving the same right answer in class, but everyone only listens to the one with the fancy new shoes. Valluvar noticed that people often ignore what poor people say, even when it is wise, and that this is unfair.
kurals.university: NaRporuL (நற்பொருள்) is ‘good matter’, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar specify as the sense of good books (nool), and nangunarndhu (‘having understood well’) stresses that the speaker is genuinely learned. Yet the soRporuL (சொற்பொருள், ‘the meaning of the words’) of nalkoorndhaar (நல்கூர்ந்தார், ‘those who have become poor’) suffers soarvu, here ‘failure, lapse’: it is not heard or heeded. The same word soarvu that meant inner weariness in 1044 here describes the social fate of the poor man’s speech, a deliberate echo. Solomon Pappaiah puts it simply: if the speaker is poor, his words are not honoured. Pope’s ‘Their sense from memory of mankind will fade away’ takes the lapse as being forgotten. The observation is descriptive and critical, not an endorsement of the bias. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that has wealth is regarded as a learned man.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna bluntly notes that society credits the wealthy with learning, and adds that a poor man is accused falsely even when he stands near.
hinduism.tie_back: If wealth is taken for learning, then, as the Kural says, the poor man’s real learning goes unheard.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong, if cynical, parallel voiced by Arjuna.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing... and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool.”
christianity.explanation: James rebukes a congregation that honours the rich visitor and pushes the poor one aside.
christianity.tie_back: The poor man is dismissed before he speaks, exactly the bias the Kural records, though James condemns it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted words); strong fit on discounting the poor, without the specific point about wise words.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they said, ‘Why was this Qur’an not sent down upon a great man from [one of] the two cities?’”
islam.explanation: The Meccan elite questioned the revelation because it came through a man without great wealth or rank.
islam.tie_back: They judged the message by the messenger’s means, the very prejudice the Kural observes.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on alquran.cloud; ‘great man’ refers to rank and wealth according to the exegetical tradition, so the link is interpretive.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So I observed: Wisdom is better than valor; but The wisdom of the poor is scorned, And their words are not heeded.”
judaism.explanation: Kohelet tells of a poor wise man who saved a city yet was forgotten, and concludes that the poor man’s wisdom is despised.
judaism.tie_back: This is a near-exact match: wise words from the poor go unheeded.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; essentially one-to-one with the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “...whoever has no conviction with regard to skillful mental qualities... no discernment with regard to skillful mental qualities is, in the discipline of a noble one, said to be poor, destitute, & penniless.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines real poverty as the lack of conviction, conscience, persistence and discernment.
buddhism.tie_back: Against the world’s habit of dismissing the materially poor, the Buddha says the truly poor are those without wisdom, a pointed counterpoint to the Kural’s observation.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org (ellipses mark omitted items); next-best match that reframes poverty rather than addressing the neglect of poor speakers.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
jainism.explanation: The mendicant, who owns nothing, must expect contempt and abuse from householders and bear it without resentment.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism assumes the poor will be slighted, as the Kural observes, and asks the voluntarily poor to meet it with equanimity.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; next-best match, about enduring abuse rather than having one’s wise words ignored.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus, disguised as a beggar in his own hall, speaks wisely to the suitors, Antinous mocks him and hurls a footstool at him; his words carry no weight because he appears to be a destitute stranger.
greek_mythology.explanation: The rightful king is scorned because of his rags, even though his speech is shrewd.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer dramatises the Kural’s observation that a poor man’s well-understood words are brushed aside.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from general knowledge of Odyssey 17, not verified against a live text in this session.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A man’s word is believed in exact proportion to the amount of cash which he keeps in his strong box.”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal’s Umbritius complains that in Rome a witness is asked first about his wealth and last about his character.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point stated almost as a formula: credibility tracks money, not understanding.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on tertullian.org; near one-to-one, though from Roman satire rather than formal philosophy.

kurals.tamil:
அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு ஈன்றதா யானும்
பிறன்போல நோக்கப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
ARanjaaraa nalkuravu eendradhaa yaanum
piRanpoala noakkap padum.
kurals.meaning: One sunk in poverty that has no connection with virtue is looked upon as a stranger even by the mother who bore him.
kurals.elementary: A mother’s love is the strongest love there is. Valluvar warns that if someone becomes poor because of bad choices and also turns away from doing right, people may turn away from him, and even his own family may feel hurt and distant.
kurals.university: The decisive qualifier is aRanjaaraa (அறஞ்சாரா, ‘not joined to aram, virtue’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as ‘poverty not in keeping with virtue’, i.e. destitution that is unrighteous in cause or accompaniment; Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as poverty without just reasons; Kalaignar makes it moral, the person who abandons virtue because of poverty. Eendra thaai (ஈன்ற தாய், ‘the mother who bore him’) is the strongest possible bond, and piRan poala (‘like another, a stranger’) marks its collapse. Read with the qualifier, the couplet does not say that every poor person is rejected, only that want combined with the loss of aram estranges even the closest kin. The ytamizh.com English explanation (‘reduced to absolute poverty’) passes over aRanjaaraa, a reminder that translations differ on how much moral weight to give it. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He that has wealth has friends. He that has wealth has kinsmen.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna says that friendship and kinship follow wealth.
hinduism.tie_back: The converse is the Kural’s picture: when wealth goes, even kin may look on a man as a stranger.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong fit on kinship following wealth, without the Kural’s virtue qualifier.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want... and no man gave unto him.”
christianity.explanation: The prodigal son, having squandered his inheritance, is left starving with no one to help, yet his father later runs to embrace him.
christianity.tie_back: The parable matches the Kural’s self-caused, unvirtuous poverty and its isolation, but reverses its ending: the parent does not treat the son as a stranger.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (ellipsis marks omitted verse); a partial parallel that pointedly contradicts the Kural’s conclusion about the parent.

islam.quote_or_event: “On the Day a man will flee from his brother And his mother and his father”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an depicts the Day of Judgement as a time when even the closest kin flee from one another, each absorbed in his own fate.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s image of a mother’s bond giving way, though in an eschatological, not economic, setting.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on alquran.cloud; next-best match, since the estrangement is caused by the Last Day, not by poverty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The poor are despised even by their peers, But the rich have many friends.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that poverty brings contempt even from one’s own circle.
judaism.tie_back: Being despised by one’s own peers is the Kural’s being looked upon as a stranger by one’s own.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; close match, though it speaks of peers rather than a mother and lacks the virtue qualifier.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A trustworthy person is the best kinsman.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada locates true kinship in trustworthiness rather than in blood or wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s qualifier, poverty without virtue, finds an echo here: it is character, not birth, that makes and keeps kin.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a loose fit on the link between character and kinship.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Mother, father, daughter-in-law, brother, wife, and sons will not be able to help me, when I suffer for my own deeds.”
jainism.explanation: The monk reflects that no relative can share or lift the consequences of his own karma.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it sees family ties failing the person who has fallen through his own conduct, but draws from this a call to detachment.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a fair parallel on kin failing one who suffers for his own deeds, though not about poverty.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as poor travellers, were turned away from a thousand homes in Phrygia before the aged Baucis and Philemon took them in.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s tale shows how readily people treat the poor wayfarer as an unwelcome stranger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The thousand closed doors illustrate the Kural’s observation that the destitute are looked upon as strangers.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from general knowledge of Metamorphoses 8, not verified against a live text in this session; concerns strangers, not one’s own mother.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...though he is destitute and begging for a bite, no one will help him with a meal, no one offer him board or shelter.”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal describes the poor scholar Codrus, whose few belongings burn and whom nobody will help.
philosophy.tie_back: Codrus, abandoned by all, embodies the Kural’s destitute man looked upon as a stranger.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on tertullian.org; a good fit on abandonment, though no family member is named and the source is satire.

kurals.tamil:
இன்றும் வருவது கொல்லோ நெருநலும்
கொன்றது போலும் நிரப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Indrum varuvadhu kolloa nerunalum
kondradhu poalum nirappu.
kurals.meaning: The poor man asks in dread: will the want that all but killed me yesterday come upon me again today?
kurals.elementary: Imagine having a very scary day, and waking up the next morning worried: “Will it happen again today?” Valluvar says a very poor person feels like that every single day, afraid that yesterday’s hunger and worry will come back.
kurals.university: The couplet is spoken in the voice of the poor man himself, an unusual dramatic touch in the Porutpaal. Nirappu (நிரப்பு, ‘want, need’) is a synonym of nalkuravu, and the particle kolloa (கொல்லோ) marks anxious questioning: ‘will it come today too?’. Nerunal (நெருநல், ‘yesterday’) and kondradhu poalum (‘as though it killed’) describe the daily ordeal as a near-death; Puliyur Kesikan adds the implied cry ‘if it comes, what shall I do?’, while Mu. Varadarasanar frames it as the poor man’s daily trembling. Kalaignar reads it as a longing that it may not return. The present-tense dread contrasts with the general statements of the earlier couplets and leads into the sleeplessness of 1049. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that distress comes and goes like the seasons and must be endured without agitation.
hinduism.tie_back: Where the Kural voices dread of yesterday’s misery returning, the Gita counsels tolerating such recurring distress with equanimity.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a counsel answering the Kural’s mood, not a parallel description of poverty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers not to be consumed by anxiety about tomorrow’s needs.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural records exactly the daily anxiety over provision that this teaching seeks to dissolve.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a response to the Kural’s fear rather than a parallel to it.

islam.explanation: The Qur’an assures the believer that every hardship is accompanied by relief.
islam.tie_back: Against the poor man’s fear that yesterday’s hardship will return, the verse promises ease alongside it.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on alquran.cloud; a consoling counterpoint rather than a description of poverty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Four are considered as if they were dead: A pauper, and a leper, and a blind person, and one who has no children.”
judaism.explanation: A baraita counts the pauper among those who are regarded as dead, deriving it from Exodus 4:19, where men who had lost their property are called dead.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural says poverty ‘as good as killed’ the poor man yesterday; the Talmud treats the pauper as one already counted among the dead.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Nedarim 64b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria (translator’s bold markup removed); strong fit on poverty as a kind of death, without the daily dread.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Happy indeed we live, we who possess nothing. Feeders on joy we shall be, like the Radiant Gods.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada celebrates monks who own nothing and yet live in joy.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s poor man fears each day’s want; the Buddhist renunciant, owning nothing, has nothing left to fear losing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a contrast between chosen and imposed poverty.

jainism.quote_or_event: “‘I get nothing to-day, perhaps I shall get something to-morrow;’ a monk who thinks thus, will not be grieved by his want of success.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches the alms-seeking monk to meet an empty bowl with calm hope instead of distress.
jainism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s day-by-day anxiety over want turned inside out: today’s lack is accepted and tomorrow is faced without dread.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close structural match (today/tomorrow want) with the opposite emotional response.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Never dare to taunt a man with deadly poverty which eats out the heart; it is sent by the deathless gods.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod calls poverty ‘deadly’ and ‘heart-eating’, a slow killer that should never be mocked.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s ‘deadly poverty which eats out the heart’ is the Kural’s want that ‘as good as killed’ the poor man yesterday.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 717-718 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong fit on poverty as killing, without the first-person dread of its return.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “...my means are less to-day than they were yesterday, and to-morrow will rub off something from the little that is left...”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal’s Umbritius explains why he is leaving Rome: each day his small means shrink further.
philosophy.tie_back: The yesterday-today-tomorrow arithmetic of want is the very rhythm of the Kural’s anxious question.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on tertullian.org; strong fit on daily recurring want, from Roman satire rather than philosophy proper.

kurals.tamil:
நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும் நிரப்பினுள்
யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
NeruppinuL thunjalum aagum nirappinuL
yaadhondrum kaNpaadu aridhu.
kurals.meaning: A man may somehow sleep in the midst of fire, but in the midst of want he can by no means close his eyes.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever been so worried that you could not fall asleep? Valluvar says that worrying about having no food or money is so strong that it is even harder to sleep than if you were lying next to a fire.
kurals.university: The hyperbole sets two ‘insides’ side by side: neruppinuL (‘within fire’) and nirappinuL (‘within want’). Thunjal (துஞ்சல், ‘sleeping’) is said to be possible (aagum) in the first, while kaNpaadu (கண்பாடு, ‘the closing of the eyes, sleep’) is aridhu (‘rare, hard’) in the second, yaadhondrum (‘by any means at all’). Puliyur Kesikan explains how sleeping in fire might be possible, through the help of mantra and medicine, and Solomon Pappaiah through yogic power; Pappaiah also narrows nirappu to the torment of hunger. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the image general. The couplet follows naturally from 1048: the dread of tomorrow’s want is what keeps the poor awake. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not disturbed in mind even amidst the threefold miseries or elated when there is happiness, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the sthita-prajna, whose mind remains calm in every kind of misery.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural observes that want makes rest impossible; the Gita holds up the sage whose peace no misery can disturb.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.56 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; an ideal set against the Kural’s observation, not a parallel to it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The sleep of a labouring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much: but the abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep.”
christianity.explanation: Kohelet says the labourer sleeps well whatever he eats, while the rich man’s wealth keeps him awake.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts tie sleep to one’s material state, but Ecclesiastes reverses the Kural, giving the sleepless nights to the rich.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; an inverse parallel that shares the theme of sleep and means but disagrees with the Kural.

islam.quote_or_event: “They were touched by poverty and hardship and were shaken until [even their] messenger and those who believed with him said, ‘When is the help of Allah?’ Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an recalls earlier believers so shaken by poverty and hardship that even their prophet cried out for help.
islam.tie_back: The deep agitation that poverty produces, the Kural’s sleeplessness, is acknowledged here before relief is promised.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on alquran.cloud; it matches the inner turmoil of poverty but does not mention sleep.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Master of the universe, I accept upon myself all the suffering in the world, but not poverty, for when I go out to the marketplace and I do not have in my possession a peruta with which to purchase, what will I eat?”
judaism.explanation: In the Midrash, Job, offered a choice, prefers every other suffering to poverty because of the gnawing question of what he will eat.
judaism.tie_back: Job’s preference for any suffering over the anxiety of want parallels the Kural’s preference for sleeping in fire over lying awake in poverty.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (the italic peruta rendered plain); strong fit on ranking poverty above physical torment, without the sleep image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Yes, young man. I have slept in ease. Of those in the world who sleep in ease, I am one.”
buddhism.explanation: On a freezing winter night on a thin bed of leaves, the Buddha says he slept well, because passion, aversion and delusion, the real fevers that rob sleep, are gone.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural says want makes sleep impossible; the Buddha shows that the one who has abandoned craving sleeps in ease even in extreme hardship.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a sharp counterpoint on sleep amid deprivation, with the burning ‘fevers’ echoing the Kural’s fire.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
jainism.explanation: Told by Indra that his palace is burning, the renouncing king Nami replies that nothing of his can burn, since he owns nothing.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural sets fire against want; Nami shows that for one who has given up possession, neither fire nor want can disturb his peace.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com; the shared fire image and the theme of possession make a strong contrastive match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, punished in the underworld, stands in water beneath laden fruit trees, yet the water recedes and the branches lift whenever he reaches for them, so he is never fed and never at rest.
greek_mythology.explanation: His torment is endless want in sight of plenty, a restlessness that never ends.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Tantalus embodies the Kural’s claim that want allows no rest, more unbearable than physical torment.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from general knowledge of Odyssey 11, not verified against a live text in this session; a mythic image of unrelieved want rather than of sleeplessness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For what sleep is possible in a lodging? Who but the wealthy get sleep in Rome?”
philosophy.explanation: Juvenal complains that in Rome only the rich can afford quiet enough to sleep.
philosophy.tie_back: The satirist arrives at the Kural’s conclusion by a different road: poverty means no sleep.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on tertullian.org; Juvenal’s cause is urban noise rather than anxiety, but the conclusion matches.

kurals.tamil:
துப்புர வில்லார் துவரத் துறவாமை
உப்பிற்கும் காடிக்கும் கூற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thuppura villaar thuvarath thuRavaamai
uppiRkum kaadikkum koottru.
kurals.meaning: When the utterly destitute do not renounce the world completely, they only become death to other people’s salt and gruel.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone who has nothing and keeps taking a little salt and soup from the neighbours, but does nothing else with his life. Valluvar says that person should either change his life completely or choose a simple life of giving things up, instead of just using up what others need.
kurals.university: Thuppuravu (துப்புரவு) means the things one enjoys or lives by, so thuppuravillaar are ‘those without any means’. Thuvara (‘completely’) thuRavaamai (‘not renouncing’) is the fault named: Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar say the only course left to such people is full renunciation, and failing it they are merely koottru (கூற்று, Yama, death) to uppu (salt) and kaadi (காடி, sour rice-water or gruel; Pope’s ‘vinegar’). Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the social point: by staying in household life they consume the salt and gruel in other people’s homes. Kalaignar reads thuppuravu as orderliness, so the subject becomes those impoverished by disorderly living. The chapter thus ends by pointing toward thuRavu (renunciation), linking the Porutpaal back to the Thuravaraviyal of the first book, and leads into Iravu (begging) in ch. 106. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “...said that poverty is for recluses. Making no provision for the morrow is a practice that suits Rishis.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna reports Nahusha’s verdict that a life without possessions suits only ascetics who have renounced the world.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s point: total want is fitting only for those who fully renounce.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Santi Parva, Section VIII (tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (opening clause trimmed); a close match on poverty properly belonging to renunciants.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Thessalonians that those who will not work should not live off others.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts object to the person who simply consumes others’ food, though Paul’s remedy is work, the Kural’s is renunciation.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; shares the concern about burdening others, with a different remedy.

islam.quote_or_event: “An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint, but you will know them by their [characteristic] sign. They do not ask people persistently [or at all].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises the dignified poor who, through restraint, refrain from begging and burdening others.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that the destitute should not become a drain on others, commending restraint instead.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on alquran.cloud; it shares the ideal of not living off others but does not call for renunciation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Skin a carcass in the market and take payment, but do not say: I am a priest, or: I am a great man, and this matter disgusts me.”
judaism.explanation: Rav tells Rav Kahana to take even the lowliest paid work rather than become dependent on others.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural condemns living off others’ salt and gruel; the Talmud insists on any honest labour to avoid dependence.
judaism.source: Talmud Bavli, Pesachim 113a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; shares the aversion to dependence, with work rather than renunciation as the answer.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that contentment with little is itself the highest form of wealth.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural tells the destitute to renounce fully; the Buddhist answer is that contentment turns having little into true riches.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a general counsel of contentment, not a call to renounce.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An ascetic should not lay by any store, not even so little as the grease (sticking to his alms-bowl); but as a bird with its plumage, so he with his alms-bowl should wander about without desires.”
jainism.explanation: The Jain monk owns only his bowl, stores nothing, and lives on what is freely given for his bare survival.
jainism.tie_back: This is the complete renunciation (thuvarath thuRavu) the Kural says the destitute should embrace instead of lingering as a burden.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong fit on total renunciation, though Jain monks still depend on householders’ alms.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Both gods and men are angry with a man who lives idle, for in nature he is like the stingless drones...”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod compares the idle man to drones who eat the honey that worker bees produce.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The drone that consumes others’ stores is the Kural’s destitute man who is death to his neighbours’ salt and gruel.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 303-304 (tr. H.G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com up to the ellipsis; strong image of living off others, with work, not renunciation, as Hesiod’s remedy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Provide things relating to the body no further than mere use; as meat, drink, clothing, house, family. But strike off and reject everything relating to show and delicacy.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus counsels limiting one’s bodily needs to bare use and rejecting everything beyond it.
philosophy.tie_back: The Stoic minimalism approaches the Kural’s call to renounce rather than to lean on others for more than one needs.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a general counsel of simplicity rather than a call to renunciation or a warning about burdening others.
